article_text:
Barbara Barrie , who received a Tony nomination for her role in Broadway’s original Company , an Oscar nomination for her performance in Breaking Away and wide recognition as the wife of Hal Linden’s police captain on TV’s Barney Miller , died October 28 at her home in Manhattan. She was 95.

Her death was reported to The New York Times by her daughter Jane Harnick, who said Barrie’s death was medically assisted and that the actor had been diagnosed with terminal cancer.

Following her breakthrough Cannes Film Festival award-winning performance in 1964’s One Potato, Two Potato , Barrie built a career that encompassed the stage, film and television, making marked contributions to all. She appeared in 11 Broadway productions, including original stagings of Stephen Sondheim’s Company , Neil Simon’s The Prisoner of Second Avenue and California Suite , Harvey Fierstein’s Torch Song Trilogy and a 2004 revival of Fiddler on the Roof .

In addition to 1979’s Breaking Away , her film credits included an uncredited role in the classic 1956 drama Giant and as the mother of Goldie Hawn’s character in 1980’s Private Benjamin.

Barrie was most prolific on television, with credits stretching back to the 1950s anthology dramas and such popular 1960s series as Route 66, The Twilight Zone, The Fugitive, Ben Casey and Ironside, among many others. In 1974 she flirted with Gavin MacLeod’s Murray Slaughter on a memorable episode of The Mary Tyler Moore Show and began her five-season recurring role on Barney Miller the following year. Her character largely was absent beyond the first season as the ABC sitcom increasingly focused on the police precinct workplace comedy rather than the title character’s domestic life.

In addition to her portrayal of Barney Miller ‘s Liz Miller, Barrie probably is best known to TV audiences for her series regular role on the 1996-2000 sitcom Suddenly Susan , in which she portrayed “Nana” Keane, grandmother of Brooke Shields’ title character. Barrie appeared in 92 episodes during the show’s five-season NBC run.

Born Barbara Ann Berman on May 23, 1931, in Chicago, Barrie was moved to New York City after college to launch her show business career. She made her Broadway debut in the 1955 play The Wooden Dish , returning four years later in The Beaux Stratagem by George Farquhar. She also appeared in various Off Broadway productions, including 1958’s The Crucible , as well as regional and touring productions.

Her signature stage role arrived in 1970 when she originated the character of Sarah in Company , starring opposite Elaine Stritch, Dean Jones and Beth Howland, among others. She was nominated for a Tony Award for the performance in what would prove to be a seminal Broadway musical.

Barrie’s most recent Broadway role was in Joshua Harmon’s Significant Other in 2017.

In film, Barrie landed her first leading role in 1964’s groundbreaking One Potato, Two Potato , portraying a divorced woman who marries a Black man and in so doing risks losing custody of her child. Both the film and Barrie’s performance were acclaimed highlights of the year’s Cannes Film Festival.

Perhaps Barrie’s most beloved and memorable film performance came in Breaking Away , when she portrayed the mother of the main character played by Dennis Christopher, a small-town young man who dreams of becoming a competitive bicycle racer. Barrie received an Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress for her performance but lost to Meryl Streep in Kramer vs. Kramer . Barrie would reprise the Breaking Away role for a TV series adaptation, earning an Emmy nomination.

Among her numerous other TV credits, Barrie appeared in Family Ties, Law & Order, Pushing Daisies, Nurse Jackie, Kate & Allie, Once and Again and Army Wives . She was Emmy nominated three times, for Breaking Away, Law & Order and Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.

Barrie was the author of two children’s books: 1990’s Lone Star and 1994’s Adam ZigZag . She also wrote two memoirs following her diagnosis of colorectal cancer: Second Act in 1997 and Don’t Die of Embarrassment in 1999.

Barrie was married to Jay Harnick, the founder and artistic director of TheaterWorksUSA, from 1964 until his death in 2007. In addition to her daughter Jane Harnick, she is survived by son Aaron Harnick and three granddaughters.

article_text:
Top AGBO execs Chris Brearton and Dominic Hughes delivered a keynote discussion at TIFFCOM , the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival , on Thursday, about how AI is impacting filmmaking, how it can be used to assist rather than replace human creators and how it will shape the future of visual content creation.

Brearton is a partner and business leader at AGBO, while Hughes is the company’s chief scientific officer and technology leader.

Headquartered in Los Angeles, AGBO focuses on producing cross-platform entertainment properties, including such films as “Extraction” (2020), “Everything Everywhere All at Once” (2022), “The Gray Man” (2022), “Extraction 2” (2023) and “The Electric State” (2025).

Brearton noted that early in their careers, AGBO founders Anthony and Joe Russo were working on the Emmy-winning comedy hit “Arrested Development” when they received a script for the show that would ordinarily be too long and expensive to produce. Instead of giving it a pass, they used digital cameras and editing to make it a reality. “They looked at technology as a solution that empowered them to tell the story they wanted to tell,” said Brearton. And that way of thinking is now in the corporate DNA of AGBO.

Another inspiration for AGBO’s business philosophy, Brearton added, was Walt Disney, who brought Disney characters to life in another medium – the theme park – for the enjoyment of fans. “In 2026 we are using technology to build a virtual theme park, a virtual community bringing people together,” he said.

AGBO also recognizes that “creative artists are special,” Brearton added: “Humans are uniquely positioned to tell stories. The way we embrace technology is all about artists and putting artists first.”

Hughes used the example of Pixar, which evolved technology around 3D rendering. “But technology was not sufficient on its own,” he said. “They used it to tell incredible stories. Technology played a supporting role. That’s how we think about these things at AGBO.”

Hughes, who has a strong academic background in algorithms and machine learning, described being an ardent fan of Disney cartoons as a child and spending his teenage years “going down the rabbit hole” of 3D rendering and video game creation. He also had a musical talent, playing cello for orchestras.

This creative side, Hughes said, has found an outlet in his career at what he calls “the intersection of media and technology.” His background informs his belief that, in creative fields, “you have to have a human that’s sitting on top and curating to make sure the algorithms are not running on their own.” At AGBO, he said, his role “is really about supporting artists to be more and more creative.”

Brearton added that AGBO wants to make sure the artists and creatives feel comfortable. “At our LA studio you’ll see our technologists and our creatives really sitting side by side, working together,” he said.

But excitement about what AI can do in supporting content creation is accompanied by anxiety about an AI-dominated future. Brearton responded that “there is a lot of misinformation” about AI’s role.

“There’s a concern that it’s going to replace us all,” he said. But what makes a favorite performance by a favorite actor special, he added, “is the human element” that AI cannot equal. “AI is really going to be more impactful, particularly in the midterm, in process efficiencies,” he said.

That is, using AI to fix problems and do work that slows and impedes the creative process. “We really think it’s an empowerment,” said Brearton. Instead of replacing artists, Hughes added, AI is “making them better storytellers.” With AI, he explained, “you can handle all the annoying things that keep you from enjoying yourself [as a creator].”

Also, the arrival of artificial general intelligence (AGI) does not mean the doom of creative artists, Hughes said. Instead, “people who are at the pinnacle of their arts” – the Brahmses and Beethovens – cannot be replicated by a machine, no matter how smart. At AGBO, he said, “the technologists are helping creatives build tools” that enhance their creativity and increase their productivity, not take their jobs.

AI, Hughes noted, is good at “regurgitating what has been done in the past,” but not good at creating something from scratch. “Machines don’t have the creativity required for that degree of novelty,” he said.

AI, however, “is good at critiquing,” Hughes observed. AI can tell you whether a play someone discovered in an attic might have been written by Shakespeare, but if you ask it to write its own Shakespeare play, “you’d have the sense that it was written by a 12-year-old,” he said.

Another example of how AI can support the creative process is scriptwriting. “If you’re struggling a little bit with a character in the third act, it can provide data,” Brearton said. “Not a solution, but data.”

AI can also help “democratize storytelling,” Brearton noted: “We’ll see new filmmakers making movies that otherwise you wouldn’t have seen” because AI has helped them achieve their vision on a budget they can afford.

At the same time, Hughes added, AI can generate endless amounts of mediocre content, “but consumers can’t possibly absorb it.” The only solution, he said, is “to raise the bar on quality,” adding, “I’m very excited about where that high quality is going to lead.”

But won’t AI replace the humans doing work beneath the highest creative levels? The people making the stage backdrops for the Mozarts? Not necessarily, said Hughes: “If you want to produce something for the ages, you need many humans involved in that loop.”

There is also the concern that AI strip-mines content without compensating its creators. But at AGBO, Brearton said, “We track every single tool and every single usage of every single tool. We’re very comprehensive about copyright and the paper trail of who did what … You have to be intentional about this. This is not ‘let’s do something on the fly.’”

The future of entertainment, Brearton said, is “concurrence.” He used the example of his son, who consumes several different media at once on his various devices. “There are four or five different sources coming into him,” he said. “That’s different from the way I would consume entertainment, but that’s the future.”

Those supplying that entertainment, he added, must have “the ability to build worlds that tell stories across all of those platforms concurrently and provide quality entertainment to that fan across those screens at the same time in a genuine way.”

“And underlying all that, you still have to create incredible stories with wonderful characters in a rich world to live in,” he said.

The keynote was moderated by Variety ‘s Asia Editor Naman Ramachandran.

article_text:
The opening in Czechia of the NHK Collection for Lidice exhibition marks a welcome opportunity for European audiences to encounter a diverse range of works from Türkiye and Central Asia for the first time.

Thirty minutes by car west of Prague, the greyscale blur of Istanbul’s spires appears proudly in Miloslav Vorlíček’s decentralised curation of 65 artworks donated to the Lidice Art Collection by Turkish-British custodian and curator of the Nahit & Huma Kabakci Collection (NHK Collection), Huma Kabakci. The photograph, Salep’ Seller in the morning light on the old Galata Bridge (1957) by Ara Güler, makes a statement in rural Czechia, where strains of Eurocentric Islamophobia worsen legacies of Western supremacy and ethnic conservatism in the heart of the European continent.

Entitled simply NHK Collection for Lidice , what sounds like an entirely bureaucratic admission of rote programming unfolds with aesthetic and multicultural breadth. The exhibition is a welcome addition to a largely unsung collection that conserves and exhibits a bold sweep of early contributions to twentieth-century art movements, including the Fluxus of Joseph Beuys and the Capitalist Realism of Gerard Richter, Sigmar Polke and Klaus Peter Brehmer.

The in-house curation by Miloslav Vorlíček, head of the collection and alumnus of the Curating Contemporary Art MA programme at London’s Royal College of Art, brings selected works from the Nahit & Huma Kabakci Collection into precious focus. The choice to foreground artists from Turkic-speaking countries bears a peculiar ring in a landscape overshadowed by the city of Prague and darkened by the first documented Nazi war crime.

In 1942, German troops razed the village of Lidice in retribution for the assassination of leading Nazi official Reinhard Heydrich, in the process executing nearly 200 men, orphaning children and sending women to the infamy of the death camps, from nearby Kladno to Ravensbrück and Auschwitz. Since its founding in 1966 by British philanthropist Sir Barnett Stross, the Lidice Art Collection has exemplified international revitalisation efforts and the value of cultural resistance in the face of gross inhumanity.

Vorlíček, who is also from a small Czech village of some 100 people, has upheld the spirit of the collection, which garnered public attention and art historical importance almost immediately when René Block responded to Stross in 1967 to make the collection relevant. At great personal risk, Block packed his Volkswagen van with art by Beuys, Polke, Richter and others before driving into Communist territory and thereby transporting the German avant-garde to the Eastern bloc.

By spiralling out further eastward, NHK Collection for Lidice challenges the art world of Czechia to look beyond its usual frames of reference. Foregoing nationalist, Western canonisation and the fleeting contemporaneities of the market, it offers a refreshingly comparative insight into regions whose artists are often overlooked, from Türkiye to Kazakhstan – a sentiment familiar to Czech artists as part of the greater Slavic region of Central Europe and the Balkans.

Immediately once inside the Communist-era gallery, ostensibly the largest edifice in the village, Untitled (2000s) by Azerbaijani painter Kemal Ahmedov conveys an expressionist talent with a range that buries the social realism of the Soviet Central Asian political order under a moonlit, architecturally organic view, a bird prominently perched on a wall, stargazing alone in a village. Beside it, Untitled (1987) by local Czech artist František Burant, which Vorlíček chose from the house collection, has a resonantly bucolic air, as a bee spreads its wings over a face-like comb of honey. The print, like Ahmedov’s oil on canvas, adapts the countrified, naturalist gaze with an emotional charge, one nostalgically dystopian and with a whiff of the post-traumatic lingering.

Figurative compositions only scratch the surface of Vorlíček’s curation, tactfully installed on wooden shipping crates to emphasise the very recent, welcome arrival of the donation to one of Europe’s more eccentric public collections. Abstraction abounds, whether in the clouding of glossy acrylic under a span of lines in Turkish painter Devabil Kara’s Resistance (2007), petroglyph-reminiscent globules of entomological antennae in Untitled (1990s) by Baku-born Altay Sadıkzade, or the crowded chaos of broadly-stroked oils in White Pulsation on a Green-Blue Background (2000) by Kazakhstan-based Uighur artist Isa Abdulkerim. The show’s range of contrasts transcends prosaic representations of cultural geography in favour of personal visions of ineffable, human transformation.

Yet, there are nods to the history of the image and the word as their forms have descended into the amorphous mutabilities of modern art since the fall of the Berlin Wall. Particularly indicative is Malevich Marlboro (1988) by Russian-American artist Alexander Kosolapov, a darling piece for Vorlíček, who admires its iconoclastic play on both Capitalist and Social Realism. There is an omnipotent irreverence in the show under Vorlíček’s roving eye, critical of ideology – whether of the East or West – and in search of more universal, artistic liberations.

Far from shifting abruptly from abstraction to modernist abandon, with the NHK donation the Lidice Art Collection is emboldening its mark on the global art map in line with its historical focus. Such pieces as those by seasoned feminist Turkish artist Ipek Duben, Kosovo I (2010) and Kosovo IV (2010), retrace seams torn by displacement in the face of armed territorial conflict. Her framing of prints on wool as delicate as flesh, battered and scarred, are no less alive than the faces they portray. By homing in on the Balkan country with tenuous recognition and embattled sovereignty, Duben’s work is a stunning reflection of the nonlinear geography of the greater Eurasian region whose artists grapple with both Western and Eastern assimilations, articulating the aesthetics of peripheral emergence in the throes of late capitalist globalism.

NHK Collection for Lidice runs until 7 March 2027

Frieze Week is a long week, with some 309 exhibitors at Frieze London and Frieze Masters in Regent’s Park alone. But if you want an atmosphere reset and are still craving art without the sound of champagne popping or air kisses, London has much to offer this season with shows such as “Renoir and Love” at the National Gallery, Tate Britain’s divisive show “ The 90s: Art and Fashion ,” “Salman Toor: Someone Like You” at the Courtauld Gallery, and “ Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends ” at the National Portrait Gallery.

London’s cultural scene, despite the country facing an upswing in right-wing politics, is still very much alive and kicking. Here are seven exhibitions that display its energy.

“Salman Toor: Someone Like You” at Courtauld Gallery Image Credit: Courtesy Courtauld Gallery Édouard Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère (1882) hangs in the Courtauld Gallery, where, next door, Pakistani American artist Salman Toor has his first European solo exhibition, “Salman Toor: Someone Like You.” In it is a work depicting a different kind of bar in The Bar on East 13th (2019), in which a man with pigtails and painted nails holds a lemon and raises it above a margarita glass. It’s one of the 19 paintings by Toor on display. There are also Phone Watcher (2022), in which a figure is dead behind the eyes with a smartphone in hand, and Fag Puddle with Carriers (2026), in which limp bodies lie on top of each other as others roam around. Until January 10, 2027.

“Renoir and Love” at National Gallery Image Credit: ©Musée d’Orsay, Dist. RMN-Grand Palais/Patrice Schmidt The works of Pierre-Auguste Renoir have made headlines recently, with several of the Impressionist artist’s paintings stolen from his home-turned-museum in southern France. (The thieves left behind two of the four paintings they tried to take; the remaining two have been recovered .) That suspenseful news story unfolded only a few weeks before the more joyous “Renoir and Love” opened at the National Gallery. The exhibition focuses on how the artist represented friendship, love, and everyday gestures across 40 paintings, from the crowded scenes in Bal au Moulin de la Galette (1876) to Danse à la campagne (1883), depicting his friend Paul-Auguste Lothe dancing with his future wife, Aline Charigot. Until January 31, 2027.

“Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legends” at National Portrait Gallery Image Credit: Courtesy the artist “Tim Walker’s Fairyland: Love and Legend,” at the National Portrait Gallery, is a who’s who of contemporary icons. The exhibition captures portraits of the Gay Liberation Front; there are also musicians such as Björk, Lady Gaga, Frank Ocean, and Chappell Roan, as well as a nude Harry Styles hugging himself. “The running theme throughout the exhibition is love—at its core this exhibition is about everyone’s right to love. It celebrates love in all its forms—the power of connection between friends, chosen families, couples and communities,” Susanna Brown, curator of the exhibition, told ARTnews recently. Walker began the project in 2020, after inspiration struck out on a walk in Highbury Fields, where he noticed a plaque tucked away on the side of a public building marking the spot where 50 earlier 150 people had gathered to protest for gay liberation. The date of the demonstration was November 27, 1970, the very same day he was born. This exhibition relays both queer history and Walker’s personal history. Until February 7, 2027.

“Robert Ryman: The Real Thing” at Barbican Art Gallery Image Credit: Courtesy Barbican Centre Before Robert Ryman turned to painting, he wanted to become a professional jazz saxophonist, and to make ends meet, he took up shifts as a security guard at New York’s Museum of Modern Art, which at the time was rapidly acquiring works by Mark Rothko, Willem de Kooning, and Jackson Pollock. The Barbican Art Gallery’s survey of Ryman’s work traces his beginnings to The Painting of the Mysterious Shadow (1966), which he created after leaving his day job at MoMA, and also includes such works as Surface Veil II (1971). The latter piece is situated in front of a bench for visitors to gather their thoughts as they gaze at Ryman’s white paint. Until February 28, 2027.

“Still Life, Then and Now” at Robilant Image Credit: Courtesy Robilant A bouquet of fresh and colorful flowers by Osias Beert the Elder, a basket of fruit by Bartolomeo Cavarozzi, a ram with its legs tied by Francisco de Zurbarán (another version was recently part of the artist’s show at the National Gallery), and a resting skull by Andy Warhol: These are among the works on show at Robilant, which is surveying the still life genre as it shifted between the 16th century and today. The gallery is also participating in Frieze Masters with a booth that holds John Singer Sargent’s Constantinople and Warhol’s portrait of Erich Marx, the German art collector and real estate developer. “We have all seen the renewed interest in Old Masters as the pendulum swings from speculative to secure, and as clients look to artists who have already shown they can hold their value,” gallery director Michele di Robilant told ARTnews . Until December 18.

“Es Devlin: Other Worlds” at Design Museum Image Credit: David Parry for the Design Museum The artist and set designer Es Delvin is a creator of worlds. (After all, she has three Emmy Awards, three Olivier Awards, and a Tony Award for production design, and has helped building sets for musicians such as Beyoncé, The Weeknd, and Adele.) In her exhibition at the Design Museum, she opens her library of work, from installations to films. She recreated her London studio and is now displaying a wall installation, titled Archive Unboxed , that combines the work she produced in her formative years in school, university and art college. The artist also partnered with Penguin Random House UK on a book installation titled Infinite Library . Exhibited at the end of the show, it includes books that will be donated to local charities. Until April 4, 2027.

“The 90s: Art and Fashion” at Tate Britain Image Credit: Courtesy Tate/Juergen Teller “ The 90s: Art and Fashion ” at Tate Britain has left art critics “dissatisfied” and “buzzing,” making it the type of exhibition you need to see for yourself. It’s a fresh and different perspective on the 1990s, and sure enough, there are works by Tracey Emin and Damien Hirst there. But the show also spotlights names not typically associated with the Young British Artists (also known as the YBAs), including Hamad Butt, Eileen Perrier, Yinka Shonibare, and Barbara Walker. Whether you walk away from the exhibition feeling empty or elated, you can let everyone know you went to the exhibition by getting one of the T-shirts that Sam Taylor-Johnson wears in her photograph Fuck, Suck, Spank, Wank (1993). You can guess what the T-shirt says. Until February 17, 2027.

article_text:
The European Film Academy has unveiled the nominations in the 16 key categories of its 39th European Film Awards taking place in Greece in January 2027.

Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland leads the nominations, making it into 11 categories, followed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s La Bola Negra with ten nominations and Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes Palme d’Or winner Fjord with five.

The nominations were announced in front of a live audience on Saturday at the Pavlos Zannas Theatre in the iconic Olympian building in Thessaloniki, as part of the Thessaloniki International Film Festival.

The winners will be unveiled at an awards ceremony on January 16 at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens, Greece, co-organised by the European Film Academy and the Ηellenic Film and Audiovisual Center.

Watch on Deadline

The nominations are based on the votes of 5,700 members of the European Film Academy who have been watching the films included in the annual European Film Awards Shortlis t, and will now vote for the winners.

Pawlikowski’s first film in eight years , Cold War drama Fatherland stars Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller as writer Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika as they travel across Germany in 1949 from Frankfurt in West Germany to Weimar, East Germany.

The Polish filmmaker shared the Cannes Best Director prize in May with Calvo and Ambrossi, whose La Bola Negra is one of the frontrunners across the award season this year.

Revolving around the interconnected stories of three gay men in 1932, 1937 and 2017 , La Bola Negra has been raking in audience awards and storming the box office at home and internationally since its Cannes world premiere and Best Director win.

Mungiu’s Fjord , starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve as a Romanian and Norwegian couple whose plans for a new life in a fjord village come up against neighbors with a very different outlook on life, won the director his second Cannes Palme d’Or this year, after 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days in 2007.

Fifteen films have garnered a nomination in the European Film category spanning fiction, documentary and animation.

Previous recent winners in the category have included Best International Feature Film Oscar winners Another Round and Sentimental Value as well as Quo Vadis, Aida? , Triangle of Sadness and Anatomy of a Fall, which won the Best Original Screenplay Academy Award.

A number of documentaries have been nominated for Best Documentary and Best film including bombshell exposé NAZA , French box office break out Whispers in the Woods and Letters from A Silenced Country . Best Animation nominees also making it into the Best Film category include festival breakouts In Waves , Iron Boy and Jim Queen .

The upcoming ceremony in Greece will be the second time the European Film Awards take place in a new January slot as part of a strategy to place them at the heart of the wider awards season, having taken place in December for many years.

The January 16, 2027 slot once again falls the day after the end of nomination voting in the Academy Awards on January 15, and before the January 21 nominations announcement. This gives European talents in the running for the Oscars time to return home to Europe for the awards. The Golden Globes will also be done and dusted with its 2027 ceremony set for January 10.

article_text:
Source: Sriya Sarkar (licensed under CC 4.0)

David Walliams

Sky has dropped family feature Fing! for UK-Ireland distribution following allegations against David Walliams, who stars in the film and on whose book it is based.

“The allegations made against David Walliams are extremely serious. We have notified the producers of the film of our intention to exit our position as the UK & Ireland licensee of Fing . We have already removed content which features him from our platforms,” said a statement from a Sky spokesperson.

Sky held UK-Ireland distribution rights to Fing! as a Sky Original title, with a tentative release date scheduled for early 2027. The film is produced by Jo Sargent from the UK with Todd Fellman of Story Bridge Films and Craig McMahon, both of Australia.

Fing! had its world premiere in the Family Matinee section at Sundance Film Festival in January. Based on Walliams’ 2021 children’s book of the same name, it follows a young girl who demands the mysterious titular creature, sending her parents on a chaotic quest through the deepest jungle.

Iona Bell, Taika Waititi, Mia Wasikowska, Blake Harrison and Penelope Wilton lead the cast, with Walliams’ regular creative partner Matt Lucas voicing the Fing.

It is directed by Jeffrey Walker, with AGC Studios handling sales. Angel Studios currently holds US distribution rights with a planned release for early 2027.

Earlier today The Guardian and ITV published a joint investigation into Walliams, in which multiple women accused the writer and performer of sexual harassment. The allegations include one woman who says Walliams initiated sexual contact with her when she was 15; there are separate allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women on ITV show Britain’s Got Talent , and at HarperCollins, Walliams’ former publisher.

Walliams denies all the allegations. The BBC has pulled all episodes of Little Britain , the sketch comedy which made Walliams’ name in the 2000s, from its iPlayer service following the allegations; while Walliams has been dropped by his literary agency Independent Talent.

article_text:
On this week’s episode of The Screen Podcast, the CEO of the British Board of Film Classification (BBFC), David Austin, discusses new research into how audiences view horror, tiered fees, and working with streamers.

Watch above or listen below

Senior reporter Ben Dalton chats to Austin about the latest BBFC polling which delved into how horror films should be rated in 2026.

“Sexual violence was the number one issue and people want us to classify that in a very strict way,” Austin revealed. “We always have done but they want us to continue to classify it strictly. The second issue that people were most concerned about was suicide and self-harm.”

The duo then discussed how classification works, why streamers operate independently and the BBFC tiered fee system.

“The idea of having that tiered fee structure is that it encourages more smaller releases, independent releases,” Austin explained. “So the UK public has its widest possible choice of films that it can go and see.”

To download or subscribe to future episodes, search for ‘The Screen Podcast’, which is available on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , Acast and YouTube .

The Screen Podcast is produced by Ellie Calnan, with Wendy Mitchell serving as editorial director. New episodes every Thursday.

The Gospel According to Paul Pfeiffer

The sculptor and video artist talks mass culture, and Nathan Fielder as performance artist?

Pop star Justin Bieber is no saint — well, actually, in Paul Pfeiffer’s art, he kind of is. In an interview in today’s issue, the sculptor, photographer, and video artist talks about his woodcarved portraits of Bieber in the likeness of Christ on the cross, his imagined million-seat stadiums, and the rituals of mass culture. “Emotion itself becomes the architecture of soft power,” he says.

All the world’s a stage. No one might exemplify that age-old adage better than the deeply contemporary (and utterly deadpan) comedian and director Nathan Fielder. Also today, Associate Editor Rebecca Schiffman takes on You Can See Everything , his new documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. “Is Fielder a documentarian,” Schiffman wonders, “or is he a performance artist playing one?”

— Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise

As an art historian, it’s hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to me recently, maybe 10 minutes into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything .

I watched Fielder hold painful, prolonged eye contact with Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster whose eerily large blue eyes seem to enact their own kind of performance. Naturally, I thought of Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” (2010). Perhaps it’s an obvious, pretentious comparison. But hear me out: Is Fielder a documentarian, or is he a performance artist playing one? | Rebecca Schiffman

Six years ago, the director of Hong Kong’s M+ museum, Suhanya Raffel, told cultural strategist András Szántó, in an interview for the book The Future of the Museum , that in the years to come museums will need to “stand together and work to help one another to deliver a more sustainable baseline.” Collaboration, she went on, “will be a key aspect of the next chapter of museum work.” Her words seem to have been prophetic: on Friday morning in Hong Kong, M+, the Museum of Modern Art in New York, and the Centre Pompidou in Paris announced a wide-ranging cultural alliance unprecedented in its scale. At the heart of the alliance is an agreement that the three institutions will treat their respective holdings as a shared collection, curated by staff spread across three continents.

“If we succeed,” Laurent Le Bon, the Pompidou’s president, told ARTnews in Paris, during a joint interview that also included Raffel and MoMA director Christophe Cherix, “we will be more than the sum of our parts, and I think that is something quite new.”

The combined holdings of MoMA and the Pompidou mean the total shared collection will number in the hundreds of thousands of objects, and the three institutions are also stewards of voluminous archives. The collection at M+, founded six years ago, numbers around 8,000 objects, but the museum has a definitive collection of contemporary Chinese art, much of it donated by Swiss businessman and former diplomat Uli Sigg. The Pompidou houses the largest modern art museum in Europe (its holdings are a national collection owned by the French state). The potential audience will be enormous: based on current figures, the museums will have a combined 10 million annual in-person visitors and 125 million online visitors.

The collection sharing will kick off with several initiatives. Beginning in late 2027, a selection of major works from M+’s collection will be installed on long-term loan in MoMA’s collection galleries, and in 2028, a long-term Centre Pompidou gallery will also open at MoMA, with similar, parallel plans in development at the other museums. (The Pompidou is currently closed for a five-year restoration of its building and is scheduled to reopen in 2030.)

As part of the alliance, the partner institutions will, over the next five years, co-organize an exhibition exploring the complex concept of “the contemporary,” which will include works from all three collections and be presented at all three institutions; curators at the Centre Pompidou and M+ will join MoMA’s C-MAP (Contemporary and Modern Art Perspectives), a cross-departmental research program founded in 2009 with the aim of exploring art histories outside North America and Western Europe.

Additionally, a joint steering committee, made up of the three museum directors along with department heads and curators from the three museums, will begin to work on such priorities as exhibitions and collection sharing, research, conservation, and professional development. The committee will meet monthly, and there will be one major in-person meeting a year, the first of which will take place next month at MoMA. (Subsequent annual meetings will rotate among the museums.)

To a certain extent, the alliance comes out of previous partnerships between M+ and the other two institutions. In February 2025, M+ and MoMA signed a memorandum of understanding that encompassed collection sharing, joint research, and curatorial exchanges. Earlier this year, M+ and the Centre Pompidou announced their own multiyear strategic partnership, which included plans for the Pompidou to inaugurate its renovated space with an exhibition of works from both museums’ collections, followed by a presentation of that show at M+.

In the interview with ARTnews in Paris, the three directors acknowledged that the new cultural alliance grew out of the previous bilateral partnerships. They stressed, however, that it also grew out of the three institutions’ commonalities, such as cross-disciplinary collecting and a focus on the art of the present, as well as the lineage the museums form: nearly a century of collecting contemporary art, starting with MoMA’s founding in 1929 and continuing through the Pompidou’s opening in 1977 and M+’s in 2021. Raffel has acknowledged that Centre Pompidou was “one of the key institutions” that M+ “looked to that helped us guide the principles around building an institution like this for Asia.” “We each have things that are absolutely unique in the world,” said Cherix. “Our first role is of course preservation. But how can we make those collections work harder for us and touch people well beyond the walls of our institutions?”

This alliance differs from past models such as traveling exhibitions, co-organized shows, and collaborations on specific projects, Cherix explained, in that it is a long-term commitment to building programs together from the ground up, one that will involve “bringing our teams much closer together.”

The new arrangement also aims to take advantage of economies of scale and to make things like shipping more sustainable. Raffel and Cherix pointed out that, for instance, sending parts of M+’s collection of contemporary Chinese art to MoMA for extended periods would not only allow those works to rotate through the MoMA galleries but also make them more easily available to other museums in the United States.

In a world in which museums want their collections to reflect global perspectives, sharing makes more sense than continuing to accumulate separately. “We can’t just keep collecting, so we are sharing instead,” said Raffel. This raises the bar for acquisitions: to be added to the shared collection, a work will, as Cherix put it, “need to have no equal” in any of the three collections.

“Even if we want to be devoted to the art of our time, we become a historical collection,” Cherix continued. “How can we reset that? I think this alliance gives us exactly the capacity to have a different scope, and a forward-looking vision.”

More museums have partnered in recent years to share collections, pool resources, and expand their audiences. The strategy has evolved from standard short-term exhibition loans to deeply integrated models that include joint acquisitions, shared private donations, regional networks, and long-term international exchanges. Joint acquisitions have become increasingly common since 2003, when the Whitney Museum, Tate, and the Centre Pompidou teamed up to purchase Bill Viola’s video installation Five Angels for the Millennium .

An arrangement somewhat similar to the MoMA–Pompidou–M+ model came in 2018, when Chinese Indonesian collector Budi Tek partnered with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) in a collection-sharing arrangement with Shanghai’s Yuz Museum, which Tek had founded. (China rejected attempts to make the Yuz Museum a public institution; Tek died in 2022.) In that case, a new foundation was formed to oversee the collection, which would live in China but otherwise travel between Los Angeles and Shanghai for temporary exhibitions. Works from LACMA’s collection, for example, traveled to the Yuz Museum in 2009 for the exhibition “In Production: Art and the Studio System,” while in 2021, 20 pieces from Tek’s collection went on display at LACMA for the exhibition “Legacies of Exchange.”

More recently, museums have agreed to be the joint stewards of certain collectors’ holdings. In 2022, around 100 works from the collection of Greek industrialist Dimitri Daskalopoulos became a shared gift to the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum and the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. In 2024, three Los Angeles museums—the Hammer, LACMA, and the Museum of Contemporary Art— jointly received s ome 350 works owned by Jarl and Pamela Mohn. Those three institutions continue to add to that collection, called the Mohn Art Collective (MAC3).

article_text:
Dal 12 al 15 novembre 2026 il Grand Palais di Parigi ospita la 29ª edizione di Paris Photo , tra gli appuntamenti più importanti per gli addetti ai lavori della fotografia e del suo mercato. Gli espositori sono 246, provenienti da 38 Paesi, tra cui 199 gallerie e 80 nuovi partecipanti. Articolata in cinque settori tematici, la fiera racconta i duecento anni della fotografia, dalle opere storiche alle pratiche più contemporanee. Come sottolinea Anna Planas , direttrice artistica, il bicentenario «non è solo un momento per guardare alla storia della fotografia, ma anche per interrogarsi sulle trasformazioni del medium». Paris Photo non propone dunque una celebrazione retrospettiva, ma una lettura che ne interroga la storia, le evoluzioni tecniche e il presente: per Planas è anche «un’occasione per accogliere collezionisti specializzati in altri ambiti e invitare un pubblico ampio a scoprire e celebrare la fotografia».

Numerose gallerie presenteranno esempi dei primissimi procedimenti fotografici, come calotipi e dagherrotipi: tra queste Gilles Peyroulet e Hans P. Kraus Jr, che espongono opere firmate da Louis Daguerre e Anna Atkins . Accanto, anche progetti contemporanei contribuiscono a celebrare l’eredità del mezzo. La galleria Christophe Gaillard dedica una personale a Isabelle Le Minh , la cui ricerca artistica indaga i confini della fotografia mettendone in discussione le convenzioni, mentre la Galerie Binome propone una selezione di opere che esplorano il rapporto tra immagine e supporto materiale.

I visitatori saranno accolti da un’installazione monumentale dedicata a Thomas Ruff , figura di spicco della Scuola di Düsseldorf che ha esplorato fin dagli anni Ottanta la fotografia dalle immagini analogiche fino alle più recenti simulazioni digitali. L’opera verrà presentata in un allestimento lungo 36 metri, realizzato in collaborazione con cinque gallerie, David Zwirner, Konrad Fischer, Mai 36, Lia Rumma e Sprüth Magers. Diverse le gallerie con sede in Italia distribuite tra i vari settori, tra cui Alberto Damian (Treviso), Lia Rumma e M77 (Milano), Matèria e Spazio Nuovo (Roma), Paci (Brescia), Serge Plantureux (Senigallia) e Spot Home Gallery (Napoli); Glenda Cinquegrana (Milano), Camilla Grimaldi (Roma) e Viasaterna (Milano).

Le altre sezioni di Paris Photo, da Voices a Digital

Curata da Francesco Zanot e Zasha Colah , la sezione Voices indaga la nozione di scomparsa. Nata per preservare ciò che altrimenti andrebbe perduto, la fotografia viene oggi esposta mentre la sua stessa forma appare in trasformazione. Si esplora la scomparsa in una duplice accezione: come fenomeno materico, con opere concepite per sbiadire e dissolversi, e come condizione di fragilità di realtà marginalizzate.

La sezione Digital , curata da Marco de Mutiis , esamina le modalità attraverso cui la tecnologia trasforma la produzione e la percezione delle immagini: «Non vediamo più esclusivamente attraverso il prisma dell’ottica tradizionale. Il nostro sguardo è plasmato tanto dagli strati di Photoshop quanto dagli algoritmi di riconoscimento facciale», dice. Emergence presenta 20 progetti monografici firmati da una nuova generazione di artisti; per finire la sezione Book , che riunisce diverse case editrici.

Non solo gallerie: percorsi alternativi a Paris Photo

Paris Photo invita il Centre Pompidou a presentare Revealing , un allestimento basato sulla propria collezione fotografica. Il programma Elles x Paris Photo , dedicato a valorizzare il lavoro delle artiste donne, è affidato quest’anno ad Aldeide Delgado e completa la programmazione della fiera, affiancandosi alle Conversazioni, ai Book Talks, ai Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards e alle sessioni di firmacopie.

Ma intorno alla fiera, oltre gli stand, si muove un sistema più ampio. Photo Days, il percorso che dal 2 al 30 novembre collega gallerie e istituzioni di Parigi e della sua regione, arriva alla settima edizione. Intanto La Bourse de Commerce – Pinault Collection prosegue fino al 18 gennaio con la maxi mostra Remember me , con circa 700 opere fotografiche di oltre 70 artisti. Musei, fondazioni e gallerie fanno così di Parigi il punto d’incontro internazionale della fotografia.

article_text:
20世紀初頭のノルウェーで最も傑出した画家の一人として、近年、世界的に評価が高まっているニコライ・アストルップ（1880～1928年）。その日本初回顧展が、東京ステーションギャラリーで11月21日から開催されます。会期は2027年1月31日まで。本展では油彩画に加え、独自の境地を拓いた木版画を含む約130点により、自然の輝きを体現したアストルップの世界を紹介します。

ニコライ・アストルップ 創造する庭

会場：東京ステーションギャラリー（東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-1 JR東京駅 丸の内北口 改札前）

会期：2026年11月21日(土)〜2027年1月31日(日)

開館時間：10:00～18:00（金曜日～20:00） ※入館は閉館の30分前まで

休館日：月曜日（ただし11/23、1/11、1/25は開館）、11/24（火）、年末年始（12/28～1/2）、1/12（火）

観覧料：一般1,800円、高校・⼤学⽣1,300円、中学生以下無料

詳しくは 公式サイト へ

鮮烈な色彩と大胆な造形が生む、独自の象徴世界

険しい山々に囲まれた西ノルウェーの湖畔の村、ヨルステル（現・スンフィヨルド）で育ったアストルップは、生涯にわたってこの地を拠点とし、天候や季節ごとに変化する自然と人々の暮らしを描きました。白夜の空に炎が燃え上がる幻想的な夏至祭、工芸品が彩る室内の情景、自ら育てた果樹やルバーブなどの植物──。とりわけ、食糧を生み出す生活の場であり、芸術的な関心を向けた創造の場でもある“庭”は、彼の芸術を体現するモティーフとなりました。

アストルップの絵画の魅力は、類稀な色彩感覚に支えられた独自の象徴性にあります。常に現実世界を描きながらも、鮮烈な色彩と大胆なデフォルメを用いて、日常の光景を、観る者の記憶や感覚を呼び起こす象徴的な画面へと昇華させたのです。また、アストルップはきわめて独創的な版画家でもありました。日本の浮世絵版画に影響を受けつつも、油彩と木版を組み合わせる類例のない手法で制作された彼の版画は、すべてが一点ものと呼べる多様性を有しています。本展では、油彩画に加え、独自の境地を拓いた木版画、再評価が進むテキスタイルデザインの仕事も紹介し、その画業の全貌に迫ります。代表作を一堂に集めた珠玉の展示空間で、北欧・ノルウェーの自然と暮らしを詩情豊かに描いたアストルップの芸術世界を堪能する貴重な機会となりそうです。

ムンクだけじゃない ノルウェーを代表するもう一人の巨匠、日本初回顧展

北欧・ノルウェーを代表する画家といえば、誰もがまず思い浮かべるのがエドヴァルド・ムンクでしょう。その17歳年下で同時代に活躍したアストルップは、ノルウェー国内ではよく知られていますが、世界的にはムンクの圧倒的な名声の陰に隠れ、長らく十分に紹介される機会がありませんでした。しかし2016年、さらに2021～22年に国内外を巡回する大規模な個展がおこなわれ、今その芸術に注目が集まっています。本展は、満を持して開催される日本初の大回顧展です。

画家であり、園芸家 アストルップ芸術の核となった〝庭〟を散策するような鑑賞体験

植物に対して並々ならぬ情熱をもっていたアストルップは、さまざまな苗木を手に入れては、自宅の庭で実験的な栽培を繰り返しました。庭は、飽くなき探究の精神に支えられた彼の芸術のメタファーとも捉えることができます。幼少期を過ごした牧師館のあるオールフースの庭と、一から開拓し、最後の住まいとなったサンダルストランの庭。画家の創作の源泉となった、二つの庭が描かれた作品群を展示します。ムンクも賞賛したといわれる、ニュアンスに満ちた緑の色彩は必見。本展のために現地で撮影された四季折々の映像を交え、臨場感あふれる空間でアストルップ芸術の真髄をご覧ください。

木版と油彩のクロスオーバー ジャンルを越境する異色の作品群を、版木とともに一堂に展示

アストルップの版画は、とても型破りでした。その最大の特徴は、一点ずつ手で加筆する、カンヴァス上で版木による摺りと手描きを併用するなど、木版画と油彩画の境界を自由に行き来する唯一無二の手法にあります。大都市の工房から遠く離れた場所に暮らしたアストルップは、すべての工程を自身でおこなう必要がありました。その結果、技法そのものを自らつくり上げることとなったのです。試行錯誤を重ねてたどり着いた彼独自の手法は、多大な労力と時間を要するものでした。本展では、アストルップの木版画や油彩画と版木を合わせて展示し、その比類ない創造の秘密をひも解きます。

芸術と育ち、暮らす 母親と協働したテキスタイルの仕事に光を当てる

アストルップの母親は、地域で主導的な役割を果たしたテキスタイル作家でした。アストルップ自身も、画家としての道を本格的に歩み始める前に、地元の植物を題材とした織物のデザインを手がけています。彼のデザインをもとに母親が織ったテキスタイルは、ノルウェー国内の博覧会で受賞するなど高く評価されました。近年、再評価が進むこの分野の仕事を紹介し、幼い頃から芸術的な手仕事とともにあった家庭環境が、アストルップの創作に与えた影響を検証します。

貴重なシンポジウムも

開幕初日となる11月21日には、本展監修者のスサンナ・ペッテルソン氏（フィンランド文化財団理事長）、トーヴェ・ ハウグスボー氏（コーデ・ベルゲン美術館シニア・キュレーター）、そして日本の巡回館担当学芸員を迎え、今回日本で初めて本格的に紹介されるアストルップの芸術を多角的な視点から掘り下げるシンポジウムが行われます。詳細は公式サイトをご確認ください。

「私はおそらく、この国でもっとも大地に根ざした画家の一人である」と語ったアストルップ。自然を愛し、自らの庭を育むように作品を生み出した画家の芸術世界を、この機会にじっくりと味わってみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

article_text:
Auctioneers estimated it would sell for over $1m, but on Thursday a Star Wars lightsaber used by Darth Vader in the famous “I am your father” scene from The Empire Strikes Back ended up selling for nearly $5m.

Darth Vader’s saber was one of 27 lightsaber props up for sale by Heritage Auctions in the US, including ones used by Ewan McGregor’s Obi-Wan Kenobi and Hayden Christensen’s Anakin Skywalker in Revenge of the Sith.

The movie prop, which was used in the 1980 film as well as 1983’s Return of the Jedi, sold for $4.875m at an event titled “the Ultimate Star Wars auction”.

The sale marked a world auction record for any Star Wars prop used on screen, Heritage Auctions said, and surpassed the auctioneer’s previous sale of Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber and severed hand from The Empire Strikes Back, which sold for $3.75m in July.

Items up for sale spanned the far reaches of the universe created by George Lucas, including an blaster used by Boba Fett and a Yoda puppet hand used during the character’s original appearance in The Empire Strikes Back.

Brian Chanes, the senior director of Hollywood and entertainment at Heritage Auctions, said the Darth Vader saber was “like the Holy Grail” to a Star Wars collector.

“It’s the one on the set,” he said. “It’s from the most iconic sequence of the entire franchise.”

Associated Press contributed to this report.

article_text:
After starring in the blockbuster biopic “Michael,” Nia Long has joined the cast of Teyana Taylor ‘s directorial debut “Get Lite.”

The Paramount movie stars Emmy winner Storm Reid and NFL rookie-turned-actor Ceyair Wright. Wright (“Space Jam: A New Legacy”) plays a talented, but sheltered, dance student who finds inspiration, love and family in the last place he expected: the subways of New York City. Reid (“The Last of Us,” “Euphoria”) is the girl who opens his life to new possibilities.

The role reunites Long and Reid after they co-starred in the hit 2023 thriller “Missing”; Long has also appeared in multiple projects for producer Kenya Barris, including his 2023 Netflix comedy “You People” and his 2020 series “#BlackAF.” She joins an acclaimed ensemble cast that features Leslie Odom, Jr., Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor, Jodie Turner-Smith, Asante Blackk, Woody McClain, Tylil James and Khayr Bullock.

Production on “Get Lite” is underway in New York City, with Taylor directing from a screenplay by Maurice Williams, based on a spec script by Eric Gross that appeared on the Black List in 2020. Paramount has slated the film for a wide theatrical release on Aug. 20, 2027.

In addition to starring in the film, Reid will produce alongside Barris and Anni Weisband for Khalabo Ink Society; Robyn Simpson for A Seed & Wings Productions, Reid’s banner; and Bill Karesh for Offbrnd. Taylor is also producing the film with Courtney “Coco” Gilbert, under their production banner, The Aunties.

Last month, Long, a four-time NAACP Image Award winner, received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame , literally cementing her status as a film and TV icon. She most recently starred in “Michael,” the blockbuster biopic about late pop star Michael Jackson, directed by Antoine Fuqua and produced by Oscar winner Graham King. The Lionsgate film grossed more than $1 billion worldwide, surpassing “Oppenheimer” as the highest-grossing biopic of all time. In the film, Long portrays Katherine Jackson, matriarch of the Jackson family, alongside Oscar nominee Colman Domingo as Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson, Michael Jackson’s nephew, as the king of pop.

Up next, Long executive produces and stars in the Netflix film “Don’t Ever Wonder,” reuniting with her “Love Jones” co-star Lorenz Tate. She is also set to star with Ice Cube in “Are They Gone Yet?“, the third film in their “Are We There Yet?” family comedy franchise, and expected to reprise her role in the next “Friday” movie .

Long’s memoir — which chronicles her life and career, including iconic roles in “Boyz n the Hood,” “The Best Man” franchise, “Soul Food,” “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air,” “Third Watch,” “Tyler Perry’s The Single Mom’s Club,” “Dear White People,” “Fatal Affair,” The Banker,” “Roxanne, Roxanne” and more — will be published in 2027.

Long is represented by Untitled Entertainment and Brecheen Feldman Breimer Silver & Thompson, LLP.

article_text:
Jusqu’au 7 novembre 2026, Elise Blanchard présente Vu de l’intérieur, l’Afghanistan depuis le retour des Talibans , une immersion de sept ans de travail sur place, au prix Bayeux Calvados-Normandie . En 2021, les talibans ont repris le pouvoir du pays. L’image devient restreinte et le journalisme est tenu éloigné. Au cours de ses années sur le terrain, la photographe découvre toutes les complexités que renferment ces lois qui forcent les Afghanes au silence. Pour autant, les images que nous avons devant nous sont celles de femmes qui se battent, un combat encore plus dur à mener à cause de leur enfermement. Dans ce pays absurde qui apprend tout de même les droits de l’homme aux petits garçons à l’école, la photographie expose la force humaine qui perdure malgré tout.

Annabelle Garbiglia : Comment parvenez-vous à capturer la force des femmes qui résistent au quotidien sans tomber dans une mise en scène héroïque ou un cliché du reportage de guerre occidental ?

Elise Blanchard : Je pense que l’important, c’est de ne pas venir avec des idées préconçues ou de se servir d’elles comme des symboles, mais plutôt de vraiment essayer de les comprendre et de les regarder. Il faut les voir chacune comme des femmes particulières. Parce qu’on dit beaucoup « les Afghanes », comme s’il y avait un type d’Afghans, mais on ne dit pas « les Françaises » à ce point-là avec une généralité aussi régulière. Donc je pense que l’effort, c’est vraiment de ne pas venir avec ces idées préconçues. Je parle d’une Afghane, mais ce que je fais, c’est rencontrer chaque Afghane dans sa situation particulière, avec son caractère particulier, son passé, ses expériences. Parce qu’évidemment, ces femmes, avec les lois des talibans, font face à des difficultés similaires, mais elles sont toutes différentes et je trouve que c’est en rentrant dans le quotidien de chaque femme et en parlant longtemps avec elles qu’on peut les photographier d’une manière qui évite les clichés.

Vous parlez des semaines passées au cœur d’une famille, où les femmes ont fini par vous considérer comme une tante. Qu’est-ce que cette assimilation familière a changé dans votre manière d’aborder les femmes afghanes dans vos images ?

Cette famille, ce sont les personnes avec qui j’ai été la plus proche dans le cadre du travail, forcément avec tout ce temps-là. J’ai commencé à connaître ces femmes à des niveaux beaucoup plus profonds que ce qu’on aurait avec quelqu’un qu’on rencontre dans le cadre d’un reportage. On rentre vraiment dans des niveaux humains qui sont les mêmes que dans toutes les rencontres humaines. Forcément, on réconcilie le fait qu’on voit une personne dans son entièreté sur le long terme. Il faut allier ces deux choses, le côté travail avec le reportage et la familiarité, et forcément, ça influence comment on écrit ou comment on photographie.

Sept ans de présence sur le terrain, c’est l’inverse du reportage d’actualité chaud. Comment en passant autant d’années là-bas, votre vision personnelle de l’Afghanistan a-t-elle changé ? Et peut-être même, comment votre vision de vous en tant que photojournaliste a-t-elle changé ?

Je n’ai pas l’impression qu’elle ait changé parce que je n’avais jamais vraiment eu de vision prédéfinie. Je m’étais attachée à l’Afghanistan via des personnes et des histoires. Mais il n’y avait jamais eu cette question, tout s’est vraiment fait naturellement. J’ai rencontré des personnes à Paris et puis des personnes pendant mes reportages. J’ai lu, et ça a toujours été par intérêt personnel d’en apprendre plus. Je n’ai jamais eu cette idée de vouloir comprendre l’Afghanistan. Ce que j’ai appris, c’est que c’est toujours plus compliqué que ce qu’on pense, on ne comprend jamais parce que ce n’est pas seulement des décennies de guerre, ce sont des personnes, ce sont des complexités et des différences qui changent constamment. Moi, ce que j’ai compris, c’était que tu peux rester aussi longtemps que tu veux, aller toujours plus en profondeur, il y aura toujours autant de nuances, plus de complexités, avec plus de personnes et d’endroits différents. Ça ne s’arrête jamais et ça ne veut pas dire que ça ne sert à rien d’essayer de comprendre, mais il n’y a jamais eu un moment où je me suis dit « ça, c’est l’Afghanistan » , j’ai toujours eu conscience que c’était toujours plus complexe que ce que je voyais.

Présenter ce travail dans le cadre du prix Bayeux Calvados-Normandie implique de parler à un public confronté à la dureté des conflits mondiaux. Qu’espérez-vous que les visiteurs retiennent de cette vision de l’Afghanistan, où la brutalité politique coexiste avec des rires, des deuils et une résistance invisible ?

Moi, ce que j’espère toujours, pour mon travail en particulier, c’est d’apporter ce que je pouvais apporter en vivant vraiment là-bas, en étant sur le terrain, en rentrant dans les nuances, dans les zones grises et dans les complexités. C’est essayer de rapporter ce que je voyais, la réalité que je voyais et surtout en étant la moins caricaturale ou la moins simplifiée possible. Vraiment essayer de refléter les personnes, de vraies personnes que je voyais et de vraies situations dans toutes leurs nuances. Parce que, quand on réfléchit, l’Afghanistan, comme on le décrit à l’étranger, comme on le décrit quand on survole simplement, ça ne peut pas être un vrai pays. C’est comme un film. Moi, mon effort, c’est d’emmener les vraies personnes, les réalités qui sont forcément bien plus complexes que ce qu’on peut croire en ayant peu d’informations depuis très loin.

Dans le contexte du prix Bayeux, qu’est ce que vous avez voulu mettre en avant dans votre travail ? Quel message précis souhaitez-vous transmettre au public occidental ?

Quand on m’a demandé de faire l’exposition à Bayeux, je voulais faire quelque chose qui n’avait pas été fait, que, moi, je n’avais pas fait non plus dans des expositions auparavant ou dans des reportages. Je me suis demandée : qu’est-ce que j’ai fait qui n’a pas été déjà fait ? Je me suis dit qu’il fallait parler du quotidien d’un taliban, dans les news quotidiennes, on ne retrouve pas ce genre d’informations. J’ai essayé de faire quelque chose qui pourrait s’ajouter à ce qu’on sait déjà. L’idée, c’était une expérience qui n’était pas prédéfinie, c’est un peu de refléter, moi, comment je l’ai vu de l’intérieur. Je suis revenue sur cinq ans d’archives, j’ai essayé de trouver les thèmes qui revenaient, les photos que je trouvais toujours intéressantes, même des années plus tard. Rien n’est chronologique, ce sont plutôt des thèmes qui me semblaient importants. Je voulais qu’on voie le contraste entre la sphère des hommes et celle des femmes, je voulais montrer comment le pays a changé et les choses importantes auxquelles les gens font face. Dans mon exposition, je veux amener une complexité, une nuance et une intimité.
